data: What questions do you have for the Government on the draft PWS? Please identify the specific section(s) if applicable.
Clarify workload, review boundaries, tools, and independence before asking firms to commit to delivery.
Please provide one relevant example of your company performing FedRAMP package review or comparable cloud security engineering work.
The examples span PMO review, independent assessment, provider implementation, and agency authorization work.

Please describe the labor mix needed to support FedRAMP 20x from end-to-end package reviews. Please identify which activities require senior engineering judgment and the qualifications or experience you would recommend for each role.
Senior judgment is widely emphasized; staffing ratios, automation roles, and delivery models vary.
Before beginning a review, how would you identify organizational conflicts of interest involving your company, affiliates, employees, or subcontractors?
Most describe pre-assignment screening; exclusion rules, lookback periods, and mitigation confidence differ.

Please explain how your personnel would determine whether a provider has adequately demonstrated a Key Security Indicator (KSI). Please distinguish among a security assertion, a security measure, evidence of implementation, evidence of effectiveness, verification, validation, and independent verification and validation. Please provide one concise example demonstrating these distinctions.
Evidence chains recur, but scope coverage, independent assessment, and the meaning of a passing check need care.

Please describe how your personnel would review a FedRAMP 20x Security Decision Record for completeness, technical sufficiency, consistency, and traceability. Please identify the evidence reviewers would expect and the conditions that would result in a question, finding, escalation, or recommendation that the package is not ready to proceed.
Four review dimensions are shared; readiness gates and class-specific requirements are less uniform.
How quickly could your team begin supporting active reviews, and how would you handle changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures during performance?
Start-date claims use different clocks; access, calibration, and change control determine comparability.

Is there sufficient expert staffing available in the Washington DC metro area to support on-site requirements with the FedRAMP team at GSA, or is remote staffing outside the DC metro area necessary to maintain the highest quality of contractor staff?
Hybrid staffing is common, but remote work ranges from optional reach-back to a necessary delivery model.

Many submissions propose a DC-based leadership or review core with nationwide specialists. That shared hybrid language masks a substantive difference: KITC, Coretec, Prudent, and others say remote staff are not necessary for quality; FITS says national remote staffing is necessary; Obsidian favors telework first. These are respondent judgments and staffing claims, not an independent labor-market study.
Explicitly recommends or proposes a combined local and remote delivery model.
Explicitly says remote staffing is not necessary or not a prerequisite, or local staffing can fully satisfy quality.
Explicitly says remote staffing is necessary or that both local and remote staffing are needed.
Expressly favors telework as the default.
Explicitly identifies scarce specialist skills or limits caused by DC-only recruiting.
Requests clearer frequency, role, notice, or cost expectations.
Contains PWS questions rather than the requested staffing-location answer.

DC has enough Rev5 and A&A talent to staff an on-site core. It is thin on 20x skills: KSIs, machine-readable data, and automation. Those people are spread across the country.

We recommend hybrid. Keep the Task Lead, the Technical Lead, and part of each pod on site. Let package reviewers and automation staff work remotely on GSA-approved devices. You get the best people, not just the nearest ones, and it costs less.

If you need full on-site staffing, ACE will hire people who live near GSA. ACE is a veteran-owned firm. We recruit through 7 Eagle Group, a veteran talent network, and Instant Teams, a military spouse talent marketplace. Both are national and searchable by location. We also use DoD SkillBridge through our talent partner. It lets a transitioning service member train on the work before they bill an hour.
Recommends a local lead/core and remote reviewers and automation staff, with full onsite hiring if required.
Frames scarcity as specific to 20x and automation, not general federal authorization talent.

Armavel can support GSA on-site requirements with qualified Washington, DC metropolitan-area personnel, including an on-site Program/Task Lead and staff needed for Government meetings, working sessions, and priority reviews. All personnel assigned on-site duties would be available to report to GSA headquarters at the FedRAMP Director’s discretion. Reporting to headquarters would not be treated as reimbursable travel.

We recommend a hybrid staffing model that combines this local presence with specialized remote personnel. This approach maintains direct collaboration with the FedRAMP team while expanding access to cloud security, machine-readable data, automation, and authorization-review specialists that may be more competitively constrained in the local market. Remote staffing also enables Armavel to recruit nationally, maintain cost efficiency, and rapidly add qualified capacity for fluctuating package volumes and urgent reviews. All personnel will operate under Government-approved access, security, communication, and quality-control procedures. Armavel will align the on-site and remote staffing mix to GSA direction, workload, and mission needs.
Recommends local leadership and nationally recruited remote specialists.
Links remote flexibility to surge, cost efficiency, and niche skills.

Yes, for the core team. Assurit is headquartered in Fairfax, Virginia, and our cybersecurity workforce and recruiting pipeline are centered in the DC metro area. The region has a deep pool of experienced package reviewers, control assessors, analysts, and program staff with federal suitability, and we would staff those roles locally with an on-site cadence set by the FedRAMP Director. Many of our staff already hold prior federal suitability determinations or security clearances, which can shorten onboarding, subject to GSA's own screening and acceptance. The pool is thinner for two skill sets this work increasingly needs: machine-readable compliance and automation engineers, and senior cloud architects with current FedRAMP 20x experience. We recommend that the Task Lead, Technical Lead, and core reviewers be DC-based, and that specialized automation and surge staff be allowed to work remotely under the same security, device, and data-handling controls. This keeps the on-site relationship the PMO relies on and widens access to the scarcest expertise.
Recommends local leads/core reviewers with remote automation and surge staff.
Identifies machine-readable compliance and senior 20x architecture as the thinner skill pools.

The DC metro area has enough qualified staff for the roles that most need to be on-site: Task Lead, FedRAMP Technical Lead, QA Reviewer and most package reviewers. The region has a deep pool of cleared and Public Trust cloud security, RMF and ATO professionals. Cloud9 is headquartered in Falls Church, VA, and its staff already support DOC/NTIS both on-site and remotely.

The scarce skills are compliance automation and machine-readable data (JSON Schema, OSCAL, APIs) and current FedRAMP 20x reviewer experience. A national pool improves both quality and surge capacity for those roles.

Cloud9 recommends a hybrid model: a DC-based core on-site on the days the Government sets, reviewers hybrid with scheduled on-site days, and a small number of remote specialists who report on-site for kickoffs and key review gates at no cost to the Government. All staff use Government-furnished devices and approved repositories, follow the same review procedures and QA, and are held to the same performance standards. Cloud9 suggests the final PWS state an on-site percentage or minimum days per week so offerors can staff and price consistently.
Recommends mostly local reviewers, hybrid scheduled days, and a small remote specialist group.
Suggests an onsite percentage or minimum days per week and attendance at key gates.

Yes. We already have sufficient expert staffing in the Washington, DC metro area to support on-site requirements with the FedRAMP team at GSA. Our proposed key personnel, Program Lead [personal name removed], FedRAMP Lead [personal name removed], Legacy/Security Lead [personal name removed], Architecture Lead [personal name removed], Automation Lead [personal name removed], and QA Lead [personal name removed], bring 15 to 30+ years of federal cybersecurity and FedRAMP-aligned experience, and current or recent work sits at DISA, DLA, NIH, CMS, and General Dynamics IT/Joint Chiefs of Staff in the DC area. [personal name removed] is based in Norfolk, Virginia, and has confirmed openness to on-site work at GSA headquarters. All six are identified, available, and positioned to support on-site days at the FedRAMP Director's discretion at no added cost to the Government.
Remote staffing outside the DC area is not necessary to maintain quality. We recommend the Government keep an on-site core for coordination and access and allow limited, controlled remote reach-back only for specialized surge tasks such as automation and schema validation, so GSA gets reliable on-site responsiveness plus deep bench strength when package volume or complexity spikes.
Claims sufficient identified onsite personnel and only limited remote surge reach-back.
Says remote staffing is not necessary; one proposed lead is described as outside the immediate DC area.

CVP maintains established presence in the Washington DC metropolitan area and is confident that sufficient expert staffing exists locally to support on-site requirements at GSA headquarters per PWS Section 8.0. CVP's USDA Cloud Security Engineering team currently operates in the DC metro area, providing on-site support to FSIS OCIO leadership and demonstrating our ability to sustain qualified, cleared personnel in the region. Our FSIS team holds active certifications including CISSP, CCSP, Security+, and Network+, and has received Exceptional CPAR ratings across all performance categories, confirming the depth of available local talent. CVP's DC metro staffing pool encompasses Senior Cloud Security Engineers, ISSOs, FedRAMP compliance specialists, and technical writers relevant to this PWS. While CVP believes DC metro staffing can fully satisfy quality requirements, we recommend the Government preserve flexibility for remote work during non-on-site periods to allow access to specialized FedRAMP 20x expertise that may be concentrated outside the region as this nascent framework matures, without compromising on-site availability when the FedRAMP Director requires in-person support.
Says local staffing can fully satisfy quality while preserving remote flexibility.
Allows remote expertise during periods without required onsite attendance.

CMIC's workforce is largely located in the Washington, DC metropolitan area, providing a local base for on-site support at GSA headquarters. We do not require remote staffing outside the region to meet routine on-site needs. We would organize delivery around a DC-area core team, with personnel available to participate in meetings, technical exchanges, and review activities at GSA when directed. Work that does not require physical presence can be performed remotely to use staff time efficiently.  

The final mix should be driven by the skills and independence required for each review. If workload or a specialized technical need requires additional expertise, remote specialists could supplement the local team without making remote staffing a prerequisite for quality. This approach provides GSA with local access while retaining flexibility to assemble the right technical skills for each package.
Proposes a local core and optional remote work or specialists.
Explicitly says remote staffing is not a prerequisite for quality.

1. Set-aside and vehicle: Will the Government consider a total small business set-aside on MAS SIN 54151HACS under NAICS 541519?
2. Workload (Sec. 3.0, 7.0, 13.0): What are the expected annual package volume, the 20x vs Rev5 mix, and the target review cycle time? Will historical volume from order 47QPCA24F0015 be shared?
3. Contract type (Sec. 7.0): Does the Government intend fixed-price review units, labor-hour, or a hybrid? How will surge (Sec. 3.8) be ordered and priced?
4. AI tools (Sec. 2.0): What does "super-intelligence tools" mean? Which AI tools are Government-approved, and may package data or CUI be processed in them?
5. Automation (Sec. 3.3): Will contractors only use Government-furnished tools, or may they propose and build validation scripts? Who owns that code?
6. Decision authority (Sec. 3.8, 4.0): For the draft certification report and scorecard, what level of recommendation (ready, not ready, conditional) does the Government expect from the contractor?
Lists PWS questions on set-asides, workload, pricing, tools, and decision authority.
The apparent staffing-location answer is under mobilization/change.

While maintaining a physical footprint in the Baltimore-Washington corridor is essential for high-touch agency governance, executive stakeholder briefings, and sensitive on-site coordination with GSA leadership, restricting talent acquisition exclusively to the Washington D.C. metro area artificially constrains access to elite cloud security and automation engineering talent.   An optimized hybrid operating model—leveraging local NCR-based leadership for on-site governance and agency coordination combined with a highly vetted, distributed remote engineering bench across strategic U.S. hubs—ensures the highest caliber of contractor staff without geographic bottlenecks. CSD’s headquarters in Baltimore provides immediate proximity to federal stakeholders while scaling seamlessly with distributed cloud expertise.
Recommends local governance leadership and a distributed US engineering bench.
Argues DC-only recruiting constrains access to specialist talent.

CybertLabs believes the DC metro area can support an on-site core team, supplemented by remote specialists to strengthen quality and surge capacity. Our talent pool includes 50+ cleared, trained, and certified cloud security engineers, assessors, and FedRAMP SMEs while our practice brings hundreds of Federal and private-sector FedRAMP assessments and NIST RMF SMEs who authored SP 800-53/53A.
To supplement this team, we would use established candidate databases such as LinkedIn, Indeed, and ClearanceJobs to identify cloud security professionals with FedRAMP experience, filtering for location, recent resume updates, and willingness to relocate. Screening would verify assessment experience, technical depth, and availability for GSA on-site support.
We favor DC-area leads and reviewers for direct GSA collaboration, with nationwide engineering, automation, and RMF specialists where authorized. Remote flexibility broadens access to specialized expertise. Final on-site commitments would reflect verified personnel availability and GSA requirements.
Proposes local leads/reviewers with nationwide engineering and RMF expertise.
Describes recruiting sources and verification of availability before onsite commitments.

The Washington, DC metro area offers access to experienced federal cybersecurity professionals, but relying exclusively on local hiring may constrain capacity for specialized FedRAMP 20x reviews. We recommend a hybrid staffing model: deploy qualified personnel on site when GSA coordination or other requirements call for it and use remote staff to broaden access to specialized expertise, support continuity, and scale with review volume. Remote work should not reduce quality; reviewers should meet the same experience and qualification standards, follow approved security and information-handling requirements, and work within a common review methodology, supervision, and quality-assurance process. This approach gives GSA access to a wider talent pool while preserving on-site support where needed. Any clearance or on-site requirements should be confirmed for the specific roles and work.
Recommends onsite support when needed and remote staff for expertise and scale.
Emphasizes common standards, supervision, and quality processes across locations.

Yes, for the core team. Devis is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, and staffed its DC-area State Department program with up to 160 U.S.-citizen FTEs. Senior FedRAMP-specific talent is scarce, and some of it sits with independent assessment services and cloud providers. We recommend handling that through per-package disclosure and recusal under PWS 11.0, so experienced assessors can review packages they have no tie to. We recommend a DC-based core (Technical Lead, Task Lead, and enough reviewers to cover on-site sessions) with remote options for surge reviewers and data engineering. That keeps on-site access when the FedRAMP Director requires it without limiting the pool for specialized roles.
Recommends local leads/reviewers plus remote surge and data engineering.
Connects access to scarce assessor talent with per-package conflict screening.

Both are needed and EY recommends a hybrid model: DC-area personnel meet on-site needs; remote staff add the depth and scale to maintain quality. EY has 260 dedicated federal practice staff with the critical mass to scale from our 1800 US-based Cyber/Digital Risk professionals. The DC-area core would lead Government engagement, coordination, consequential reviews, QA, and escalations, and report on-site when required. Our remote personnel would provide scalable capacity for evidence processing, structured validation, traceability, issue tracking, and selected technical analysis, extending, not replacing, local presence. Tier 1 would need not be DC-based; SI-assisted review lets practitioners focus on exceptions and judgment. EY would route work by expertise and add qualified staff from its national bench. EY uses this model on DOE assessment and authorization work across a 140+ system portfolio. Distributed support would follow GSA security, data-handling, access, facility, and telework requirements. This gives GSA local access, specialized expertise, scalable capacity, and an efficient staffing mix ad volume changes.
Says both are needed: local leadership and remote capacity, including non-DC Tier 1 work.
Uses distributed staffing as a central scaling model rather than rare specialist reach-back.
“Hybrid” does not mean agreement on necessity

Yes. We recommend a DC-based core team working on site at GSA headquarters, supplemented by remote SMEs. Our FedRAMP assessors live and work in the DC metro area, including penetration testers with active clearances, and Excentium holds a Top Secret facility clearance. We have staffed on-site federal teams locally, including a 28-person Secret-cleared team at Navy BUMED headquarters in Falls Church and its detachments, and the Space Force Mission Support Office in Arlington.

The scarcest skills are 20x-specific: KSI and persistent-validation review, and automation engineering for machine-readable compliance data. Many of the strongest practitioners work remotely for providers and assessors nationwide. Government-approved remote specialists can expand access to particular cloud platforms, automation, and emerging technologies. They would support DC-based leads. We have surged before: for DHA's Desktop-to-Datacenter migration, we staffed an average of 18 TS-cleared ISSOs and administrators across 10 states, with no corrective actions.

We would plan required GSA attendance without separate travel reimbursement, as the draft PWS specifies.
Recommends local assessors and leadership with nationwide 20x/automation specialists.
Draws on distributed surge experience while retaining a DC-based core.

FITS believes that remote staffing outside of the DC metro area is necessary to maintain the highest quality of contractor staff and to manage costs. This style of review requires deeper technical expertise than the legacy FedRAMP and FISMA style of Authorization to Operate package review required, with personnel coming from cloud engineering and software development background. Management functions could certainly be performed onsite in the Washington DC Metro area.
Says remote staffing is necessary for the highest-quality technical staff and cost management.
Would keep management onsite, distinguishing engineering delivery from local coordination.

Yes. GRAHAM confirms it can staff qualified personnel in the Washington, DC metropolitan area to meet GSA-directed on-site requirements. We propose a DC-centered team for task leadership, senior cloud security engineering, package review, QA, Government meetings, and sensitive decisions. Our ongoing DHS USCIS G-CACS III work demonstrates cybersecurity assessment delivery for National Capital Region stakeholders, and our recruiting/onboarding capability supports mobilization within 30 days, subject to GSA access and onboarding. Specialized automation and machine-readable evidence personnel can also be staffed locally; remote expertise is an option only when GSA permits it, not a prerequisite for meeting on-site requirements. Under a Government-approved approach, CCI-based automation would reduce repetitive evidence processing so qualified local reviewers can concentrate on technical sufficiency, exception resolution and risk. We would finalize specific assignments and schedules against GSA's on-site direction and final staffing qualifications.
Says even automation specialists can be staffed locally, with remote work optional.
Presents local capacity as sufficient and approved automation as a way to reduce repetitive work.

Guidehouse recommends a DC-metro-based core team able to report to GSA headquarters as directed, with Government-approved remote specialists used selectively for niche expertise, scale, or surge. Our documented cybersecurity delivery includes NIH CIT work in MD, DOJ cybersecurity support in DC, and State Department cyber risk work in VA. This provides relevant regional delivery experience and proof of our ability to staff large cyber programs in the DC metro area. We would establish a candidate pipeline of available, conflict-free FedRAMP 20x specialists to support this work. 
Remote staffing outside the region should be an option to have access to a larger, more cost-efficient talent pool. Before committing staffing levels, we would validate availability, engineering qualifications, independence, screening, and ability to meet on-site expectations. We recommend defining required on-site roles, frequency, notice, and core hours so offerors can propose comparable staffing. Any remote arrangement would require Government approval and follow compliant access/data handling and security requirements.
Recommends a DC core and selective remote expertise, with verified availability.
Requests role, frequency, notice, and core-hour definitions before firm commitments.
Location is also a pricing question

Yes for the core team. The Washington DC area has a deep pool of federal cloud security and RMF staff, and IBSS, headquartered in Silver Spring, MD, draws its cyber bench from it. The specific 20x skill set, KSI and Security Decision Record review with machine-readable data, is thin everywhere, so limiting recruiting to the metro area narrows an already narrow pool. A hybrid model keeps quality highest: a DC-based core (Task Lead, Senior Cloud Security Engineer, QA Reviewer, and a rotation of Package Reviewers) available on site at GSA headquarters at the FedRAMP Director's discretion, with specialist reviewers and the automation engineer working remotely from within the United States under the screening and data-handling rules in Section 10.0. Remote reviewers also supply the surge capacity in Section 3.8 without adding on-site seats. IBSS recommends the solicitation require DC-area presence for named on-site roles only and permit remote performance for the rest.
International Business Sales And Services Corp (IBSS Corp)
Recommends named local roles and remote specialist/reviewer capacity.
Explicitly proposes requiring DC presence only for designated onsite roles.

Yes. KITC can recruit and staff qualified cybersecurity and cloud security professionals from the Washington, DC metropolitan area to support GSA’s on-site FedRAMP 20x review requirements. Drawing on our established federal cybersecurity practice and network of qualified technical professionals, KITC can identify and recruit personnel with expertise in cloud security engineering, security control assessments, NIST RMF, authorization support, continuous monitoring, and technical evidence evaluation.

KITC would prioritize DC-area personnel for positions requiring regular interaction with the FedRAMP PMO, including technical leadership, senior security reviewers, and program coordination. We do not anticipate that staffing outside the DC metropolitan area would be necessary to maintain a high-quality review team. However, we would retain flexibility to supplement local personnel with specialized remote expertise where permitted by GSA and beneficial to the requirement.

Final staffing would be aligned with GSA’s qualifications, security screening, and on-site expectations.
Says a high-quality local team is feasible and remote expertise is optional.
Explicitly disagrees with treating remote staffing as necessary for quality.

Yes. LDR’s experience shows sufficient expert, cleared cybersecurity talent in the Washington DC metro area to staff on-site requirements with the FedRAMP team at GSA. LDR supports federal programs in Washington, DC (Dept of Interior, Internal Revenue Service Bureau of Engraving and Printing) and Bethesda, MD (National Cancer Institute (NCI)), and continues at NCI under a new five-year Enterprise Cyber Security Services task order. LDR’s ability to onboard cleared staff quickly and to surge, as described in our response to Question 6, supports both an initial team and additional capacity when on-site presence is directed.

DC-based staffing is the better model for this work: on-site presence can be directed at short notice, and close daily coordination with the Government Task Lead supports review quality. For rare specialty skills not available locally, LDR can support remote staff by applying the same screening and qualification standards as on-site staff, limiting work to Government-approved systems and repositories, aligning hours with the GSA team, and keeping remote reviewers under the same QA, tracker and traceability controls.
Prefers DC-based staffing with rare remote specialty exceptions.
Places greater weight on short-notice attendance and daily coordination than the telework-first response.

Yes, the Washington DC metro area contains a large pool of qualified FedRAMP, cloud security, and cybersecurity professionals capable of supporting on-site requirements. However, limiting staffing solely to the local market can restrict access to highly specialized expertise, increasing competition and cost for talent. We recommend a hybrid staffing approach that maintains a strong on-site presence in the DC area while leveraging remote subject matter experts nationwide for specialized skills, surge support, quality assurance, and continuity of operations. This model provides access to the highest quality personnel, improves staffing flexibility, and reduces hiring risk and cost, all while ensuring responsive support to the FedRAMP team. By combining local resources with remote experts, we can meet on-site requirements while maximizing access to experienced FedRAMP reviewers, cloud security engineers, and assessment specialists.
Recommends local presence with nationwide specialists for expertise, surge, and continuity.
Connects national recruiting to cost and hiring risk rather than claiming local staffing is impossible.

Longevity anticipates meeting core on-site requirements through qualified cybersecurity, FedRAMP, and program management personnel in the Washington, DC metropolitan area, with the flexibility to supplement these resources through a qualified 3PAO partner. Our relationships with multiple assessment organizations provide access to specialized reviewers with appropriate qualifications, availability, and independence.
Flexibility to engage qualified SMEs and reviewers outside the DC metro area would expand the available talent pool, strengthen access to specialized cloud security expertise, and enhance surge capacity during periods of increased package volume or complex technical reviews. With Government approval, remote specialists could augment local staff without compromising quality or accountability.
Longevity would maintain a staffing roster, designate senior technical and independent QA responsibilities, and align personnel with package complexity and OCI eligibility. All reviewers would use Government-authorized systems and comply with applicable security and data-handling requirements. On-site coverage would be aligned with GSA's direction.
Proposes local coverage supplemented by qualified assessment partners and remote SMEs.
Conditions assignments on qualifications, availability, and package-specific independence.

Requiring every role to be DC-based would narrow the specialist pool without improving review rigor, since package review is performed in Government-approved systems regardless of location.
Recommends local leads, QA, and program staff with remote specialist reviewers/data staff.
Distinguishes specialist quality from routine geographic presence.

Key roles, including the Program Manager, Deputy PM, and senior technical leads, are based in the DC metro area, enabling in-person collaboration with GSA. Recommends telework first with DC attendance for meetings and directed work.

Yes, the DC metro area has sufficient expert staffing, so remote staffing outside the region is not necessary to maintain quality. FedRAMP Definitions establish a shared understanding for terms when the plain-language meaning is not precise enough to support consistent use across the rules. When a defined term appears in a rule, the definition is a critical part of that rule and must be followed precisely, even if the term is commonly used differently elsewhere; when no definition exists, the plain-language meaning is expected.

This requires reviewing the actual measures themselves at a technical level, such as reviewing underlying code as appropriate; don't simply review documentation or screenshots.
Assessors MUST verify that the measures implemented by the cloud service offering matches the measures they documented to meet FedRAMP Practices.
Assessors MUST validate the effectiveness of the implemented measures to ensure they have the intended outcome for meeting FedRAMP Practices.

For example, if the documentation says that firewall rules are used to block traffic then the cloud service provider would verify that firewall rules are in place to block traffic and supply that evidence to assessors (preferably by allowing them to see how firewall configurations are deployed from a source of truth).
Providers MUST supply evidence to all necessary assessors of the implementation of the measures that have been documented to meet FedRAMP Practices; this evidence is the result of verification.

For example, after verifying that firewalls are configured to block traffic following IVV-CSO-SEI (Supply Evidence of Implementation), the provider would validate that traffic is actually being blocked and supply evidence of that validation to assessors (such as by allowing them to see metrics on the traffic that is blocked vs not).
Providers MUST supply evidence to all necessary assessors of the effectiveness of the measures that have been implemented to meet FedRAMP Practices; this evidence is the result of validation.
